evidence: src/infrastructure/http-app.ts: createApp sends every route through OrderService (stockLevels, addProduct, placeOrder, listOrders, getOrder, advance, cancel). It does not touch the repositories.
src/infrastructure/http-app.ts: ACTIONS only maps URL action names to target OrderState values. The rules for which transitions are allowed stay in service.advance.
src/infrastructure/http-app.ts: STATUS maps DomainError codes to HTTP status codes, which is translation logic that belongs to the adapter.
src/infrastructure/in-memory-repositories.ts: InMemoryProductRepository implements ProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository implements OrderRepository. Both are simple Map-backed stores.
src/infrastructure/server.ts: builds OrderService with the in-memory repositories, seeds data through service.addProduct, and calls createApp(service).listen.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The module holds the infrastructure adapters plus the composition root. In http-app.ts, createApp is the HTTP adapter and talks to the application only through OrderService. In in-memory-repositories.ts, InMemoryProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository implement the application ports. server.ts wires these together and starts the server. These three roles belong to one concern: adapting the application to the outside world. The HTTP file maps routes to service calls (ACTIONS) and error codes to statuses (STATUS). It does not rebuild the order state machine or stock rules, so nothing is decided in two places. The 'items must be an array' check only checks the shape of the HTTP request before the domain sees it. server.ts adds seed products through service.addProduct instead of writing to the repositories directly, so it uses the module's abstractions. The two repository classes look alike, but each implements a different port, so this is not duplicated logic.
